thinking_and_logic: The implemented logic iterates over the array and collects indices where nums[i] equals target. Two Sum instead requires finding two distinct indices whose values add to target; this requires reasoning about complements (target - nums[i]) and ensuring you don’t reuse the same element twice. The failed tests (basic pair, pair at end, duplicates, negative numbers, two elements) are all consistent with not checking sums of pairs.
code_assessment: Your final code does not implement Two Sum; it implements 'find all positions where the element equals the target'. The canonical optimal solution uses a single-pass hash map (value -> index) and checks whether the complement has been seen before inserting the current value. That pattern correctly handles duplicates and negatives and returns immediately when the unique pair is found; your approach cannot find any pair unless one of the numbers itself equals target (which is not what the problem asks).

next_steps.action: Re-implement Two Sum using the single-pass hash map complement pattern (seen[value] = index; if complement in seen: return [seen[comp], i]).
next_steps.why: This is the canonical optimal approach (O(n) time, O(n) space) and directly addresses the core requirement of finding a pair sum while handling duplicates/negatives correctly.
next_steps.how: Write it from scratch, then test manually on: [2,7,11,15],9; [3,3],6; [-1,-2,-3,-4,-5],-8; and a case where the pair is at the end.

next_steps.why: Your main miss was spec interpretation; this habit prevents spending the whole time coding the wrong function.
next_steps.how: On each problem, explicitly write: 'need i!=j, nums[i]+nums[j]=target, return indices' and confirm with a sample input/output before typing code.
